etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to rise, arise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to stir, rise”). See also raise.

definitions.definition: To move upwards.
To grow upward; to attain a certain height.
To slope upward.
(of a celestial body) To appear to move upwards from behind the horizon of a planet as a result of the planet's rotation.

quote.citation: [1898], J[ohn] Meade Falkner, Moonfleet, London; Toronto, Ont.: Jonathan Cape, published 1934, →OCLC:
quote.text: And still the hours passed, and at last I knew by the glimmer of light in the tomb above that the sun had risen again, and a maddening thirst had hold of me. And then I thought of all the barrels piled up in the vault and of the liquor that they held; and stuck not because 'twas spirit, for I would scarce have paused to sate that thirst even with molten lead.

definitions.definition: To become erect; to assume an upright position.
To leave one's bed; to get up.

quote.text: Yellow is the colour of my true love's hair,In the morning, when we rise

definitions.definition: (figurative) To be resurrected.
(figurative) To terminate an official sitting; to adjourn.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter X, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: It was near nine […] before the House rose.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move, or appear to move, physically upwards relative to the ground.
To attain a higher status.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall.

quote.citation: 1846, Julius Hare, The Mission of the Comforter:
quote.text: among the rising theologians of Germany

definitions.definition: Of a quantity, price, etc., to increase.

quote.citation: 2013 July 6, “The rise of smart beta”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8843, page 68:
quote.text: Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in many developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.

definitions.definition: To become more and more dignified or forcible; to increase in interest or power; said of style, thought, or discourse.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self again; […] . Our table in the dining-room became again the abode of scintillating wit and caustic repartee, Farrar bracing up to his old standard, and the demand for seats in the vicinity rose to an animated competition.

definitions.definition: To ascend on a musical scale; to take a higher pitch.
(intransitive) To increase in value or standing.
To become active, effective or operational, especially in response to an external or internal stimulus.

quote.citation: 2011 December 16, Denis Campbell, “Hospital staff 'lack skills to cope with dementia patients'”, in Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: Professor Peter Crome, chair of the audit's steering group, said the report "provides further concrete evidence that the care of patients with dementia in hospital is in need of a radical shake-up". While a few hospitals had risen to the challenge of improving patients' experiences, many have not, he said. The report recommends that all staff receive basic dementia awareness training, and staffing levels should be maintained to help such patients.

definitions.definition: To develop, to come about or intensify.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XV, page 24:
quote.text: To-night the winds begin to rise⁠And roar from yonder dropping day:⁠The last red leaf is whirl’d away,The rooks are blown about the skies; […]

definitions.definition: To swell or puff up in the process of fermentation; to become light.
(of a river) To have its source (in a particular place).

quote.citation: 1802 December 1, “Interesting description of the Montanna Real”, in The Monthly magazine, or, British register, Number 94 (Number 5 of Volume 14), page 396:
quote.text: The majestic Marannon, or Amazon River, rises out of the Lake Launcocha, situated in the province of Tarma, in 10° 14ʹ south latitude, and ten leagues to the north of Pasco.

definitions.definition: To become perceptible to the senses, other than sight.
To become agitated, opposed, or hostile; to go to war; to take up arms; to rebel.

quote.text: No more ſhall nation againſt nation riſe, / Nor ardent vvarriours meet vvith hateful eyes,  […]

definitions.definition: To come to mind; to be suggested; to occur.

quote.citation: 1714 July 20 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison], “FRIDAY, July 9, 1714”, in The Spectator, number 565; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume VI, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: A thought rose in me, which I believe very often perplexes  […] men of contemplative natures.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: To begin, to develop; to be initiated.
(transitive) To go up; to ascend; to climb.
(transitive) To cause to go up or ascend.

quote.citation: 1882, William Clark Russell, My Watch Below:
quote.text: Until we rose the bark we could not pretend to call it a chase.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To retire; to give up a siege.

quote.citation: 1603, Richard Knolles, The Generall Historie of the Turkes, […], London:  […]  Adam Islip, →OCLC:
quote.text: He, […]  rising with small honour from Gunza, […] was gone.

definitions.definition: To come; to offer itself.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 59:
quote.text: There chaunced to the Princes hand to rize, / An auncient booke,  […]

definitions.definition: (printing, dated) To be lifted, or capable of being lifted, from the imposing stone without dropping any of the type; said of a form.
The process of or an action or instance of moving upwards or becoming greater.
The process of or an action or instance of coming to prominence.
(chiefly UK, also Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa) An increase in a quantity, price, etc.
(UK, Ireland, Australia, rest of Commonwealth, sometimes Canada) Ellipsis of pay rise: an increase in wage or salary.
The amount of material extending from waist to crotch in a pair of trousers or shorts.
(Sussex) A small hill; used chiefly in place names.
An area of terrain that tends upward away from the viewer, such that it conceals the region behind it; a slope.

quote.citation: 2019 November 21, Samanth Subramanian, “How our home delivery habit reshaped the world”, in The Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: the land rolls gently, so that, upon cresting a low rise or passing a copse of wind turbines, you suddenly spot a lot full of lorries or a complex of gigantic sheds.

quote.citation: 1884 December 10, Mark Twain [pseudonym; Samuel Langhorne Clemens], “Chapter VII”, in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn: (Tom Sawyer’s Comrade) […], London: Chatto & Windus, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: I went along up the bank with one eye out for pap and t'other one out for what the rise might fetch along.

definitions.definition: (informal) A very noticeable visible or audible reaction of a person or group.
(architecture) The height of an arch or a step.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ris, rys, from Old English hrīs, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą (“twig; shoot”). More at rice.

definitions.definition: Alternative form of rice (“twig”)
